articles.title: A massive heat dome is bringing storms to the Northeast, and causing sweltering temperatures heading into fall
articles.summary: A round of severe storms and flooding is taking aim at the Northeast by middle of next week, fueled by a heat dome settling over the southeast.
articles.body: The Southeast is roasting under a heat dome that’s set to send several rounds of severe storms and flooding to the Northeast and Great Lakes this week. Fall will be here soon, but it won’t feel like it across much of the South and central US, where a heat dome stretching from the Rockies to the East Coast has pushed temperatures above 100 degrees over the past week, especially in Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Louisiana and Arkansas. Combined with the humidity, some days have felt closer to 110 degrees. The heat itself may not set many record highs in the next few days, but overnight lows are expected to be 10 to 15 degrees above average, with some spots as hot as 20 degrees above. Well over 100 record-warm daily lows could be broken over the next week. But the heat dome, an area of high pressure that traps warm air beneath it, isn’t just sending temperatures soaring. It’s also feeding a storm threat facing the Northeast and Great Lakes starting Tuesday in two ways. First, it acts like a boulder in the jet stream, obstructing the normal flow of air and sending storms riding up and around its edges. It’s similar to the setup that fueled deadly flooding across the Plains and Midwest earlier this month. It also sharpens the temperature contrast between the hot air it’s trapping and cooler air to its north and east. That contrast creates spin in the atmosphere, which developing storms can draw on to organize and strengthen. The first flooding rain threat begins Sunday afternoon and continues overnight into Monday, with the heaviest rainfall tracking through Pennsylvania and New York State into New Jersey and New York City overnight. Rain is already falling in the Midwest Sunday morning from Chicago to Detroit, and it could start moving east around 6 p.m., reaching New York City by 10 or 11 p.m. Two to 3 inches of rain are possible in a corridor stretching from the Great Lakes into southern New England, though confidence is low on how far east the rain will travel. More rounds of rain and flooding are likely Tuesday through Thursday somewhere in the Northeast, but confidence is low on exactly where those storms will set up. As the planet heats due to climate change, our warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture and fuel heavier, more frequent downpours.

articles.title: Notting Hill Carnival's 60th year celebrated on family day
articles.summary: Crowds take to the streets of west London to enjoy family day in the bank holiday weekend sunshine.
articles.body:
As I walk into the heart of the 60th Notting Hill Carnival, the sun is shining and bouncing off the sequins, gems and sparkles of the costumes and decorations surrounding me.

Flags from all over the Caribbean and Africa have been hung from the windows of the houses and are draped over the shoulders of people passing by.

Everyone is dressed for sunshine, despite the rain that was forecast. It seems the spirit of Carnival has seen off those dark clouds.

The Sunday parade hasn't started yet, but the music is already pumping, and plenty of people are dancing, already covered in paint from J'ouvert, the traditional early-morning celebration which kicks off Sunday's festivities.

Today is all about families and the children. And they have certainly got the memo. There are children everywhere, all ready for the fun of the day.

Toddling past me is surely one of Notting Hill Carnival's youngest visitors. Triny-Savannah is just 18 months old, and is here with her mum Twinsy, all the way from Paris.

"It means a lot to be here," Twinsy says. She explains that her parents used to bring her and her twin sister, and now she's carrying on the tradition with the next generation.

"It's the celebration of the abolition of slaves, so it's a big day of memories," Twinsy says.

Sitting on the pavement nearby I spot eight-year-old Alex and his mum, Tiana. I soon find out it's Alex's first Carnival.

He has the biggest smile on his face and a water pistol loaded with paint.

"I haven't been for a long time," Tiana, from Enfield, explains, "but when I was younger I used to come religiously every year and it's nice to come back with Alex."

I ask Alex how he feels about the whole morning, and he says: "I love it. It's really busy, but then it's also like we're all together at the same time, so that's great."

Before the parade starts, I go in search of a snack and find a food stall tucked away from all the crowds.

The man being served ahead of me, Dave, bites into his snack and he's instantly in heaven.

"When I bite into this, I feel like I'm about to land in Trinidad and I'm looking out of the window at the beauty," he says, still with his eyes closed, imagining it.

He's eating "doubles", a street food snack of flatbreads filled with curried chickpeas.

The woman serving, Christina Bedau, asks if I want to try it. Of course I do. But, hold the extra spice please, as I'm useless with anything too hot.

Christina hands me her creation, and it looks great. When I taste it, I can see what Dave means, although, I think to make it a fair comparison, I should probably fly to Trinidad just to check he's being accurate.

Christina has been coming to Notting Hill Carnival with her food stall, Sweet Hand Cuisine, for the past seven years. She says she "has to come" because if she didn't, the regulars who come back every year would be "up in arms".

She estimates she'll sell at least 500 doubles this weekend.

Now the parade is well under way, and the swell of sound is all around us in the form of booming sound systems passing by on huge trucks, as well as dancers and steelpan groups.

Sunday's event is a much smaller version than the huge parade that will be here tomorrow, but this is still very impressive, and beautiful.

Heather is part of one of the passing floats, and tells me she is a steelpan player, although today she's "just partying" on her float.

"I arrived in this country in 1992 and I've been to every Carnival [since]," she says.

"This is about recharging and being immersed in my culture.

"We work hard and we want to play hard and just enjoy our culture," she explains before she disappears back into the crowd.

I spot a stall selling beautiful fans, and stop to buy one for my daughter. It's handmade, from Ghana, and Betty, who sells it to me, says it's made of cotton.

I then try to show Betty how to take card payments on her phone. But, it's already getting busy, so she may just have to rely on those with cash.

There will be around two million people visiting this part of west London for the carnival this weekend.

It is Europe's largest street festival and the second-largest carnival in the world, surpassed only by Rio de Janeiro's Carnival in Brazil.

It doesn't matter how many times I come to Carnival, I am always surprised at the complete transformation of this area. It's almost unrecognisable.

The floats travelling past me are full of life and music. I could take photos of this all day long.

The family next to me catch my eye, all kitted out in matching St Vincent's outfits.

Daniel's five-year-old son Asher has already got tired legs, so he's popped him on his shoulders. It could be a long day for Daniel's shoulders.

Daniel explains that his wife, Rachel, is from the Caribbean island and they have all just returned from their first family holiday there.

"It's great to represent St Vincent here," Daniel says. "This is a perfect kind of event," he adds.

I say goodbye to the family and realise the time. I have to head off to write about my day. I take another 50 photos, at least, on the walk back to Paddington station.

I spot a poster as I leave, which says: "Fund 60 more," and asks people to donate money, to keep Carnival going.

I wonder what Carnival will look like in another 60 years? Perhaps some of the children I met today will remember this big milestone for the festival, and tell their children about today, in another 60 years.

articles.title: Rival Libya factions sign deal to hold national elections within two years
articles.summary: Signing takes place at UN mission in Tripoli after initial draft inked by UN-backed committee in Tunis on August 20.
articles.body:
Representatives of Libya’s rival governments have signed a deal to hold national elections within two years after years of political divisions.

The agreement, signed on Sunday, says legislative and presidential elections will be held under a single executive authority within a “period not exceeding 24 months”, according to Walid Ellafi, state minister of political affairs and communications in the internationally recognised Government of National Unity, based in Tripoli.

The signing ceremony took place in Tripoli at the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) after the UN-backed “4+4 committee” signed an initial draft in Tunis on August 20.

The committee consisted of four representatives from the House of Representatives, based in eastern Libya, and four representatives from the High Council of State, linked to the Government of National Unity in the west.

Libya has been divided since 2014 between two opposing administrations: the internationally recognised government and an eastern administration backed by renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar.

Shibani AbuHamoud, head of the general delegation of Haftar’s forces, said it would work with UNSMIL on a “framework within one month of the signing of the agreement to follow up on all matters related to its implementation”.

However, the agreement notes that if the House of Representatives and the High Council of State do not approve the deal within a month, it would be adopted nationally by the parties as a constitutional document and would receive international support through the UN Security Council.

Scepticism, however, remains over the success of the agreement, and analysts said the real problem of who governs Libya in the interim remains because they would control the country’s resources and have to deal with a sensitive security environment.

While the UN and other mediators have been trying to unify the country since 2011 after a rebellion toppled and killed leader Muammar Gaddafi, implementation continues to be the biggest challenge. A presidential election has been repeatedly stalled due to political disputes.

articles.title: IISc eco-friendly foam moves from lab to market; TOI story drew industry
articles.summary: India News: BENGALURU: An eco-friendly bio-based foam developed by researchers at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), is moving from the laboratory towards co.
articles.body: BENGALURU: An eco-friendly bio-based foam developed by researchers at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), is moving from the laboratory towards commercialisation, with Absolute Cold LLP working on its use in cold-chain and temperature-controlled packaging.The foam, developed by Prof Suryasarathi Bose and Prof Subodh Kumar, along with the team comprising Sampath Parasuram, Akshay Sunil Salvi, Supriya H, Sandeep Kumar Singh and Amit Malakar, is an alternative to conventional polyurethane (PU) foam, which is widely used for insulation but is difficult to recycle after use.The IISc material was designed to combine the properties needed for insulation with a more sustainable approach to what happens to the material at the end of its life. The journey from laboratory to industry also had a link to TOI.Bose said a report on the development published by TOI on Nov 11, 2024, helped bring a potential industry partner on board. “Your [TOI] article brought in a potential licensee on board and helped take the technology to market. Absolute Cold director saw your story and reached out to us,” he said.The original IISc work involved making the foam using epoxidised fatty acids derived from non-edible oils and polyphenol-based materials derived from tea leaves. The researchers also incorporated a chemical structure that allows the material to be reprocessed, rather than simply being discarded after use.Absolute Cold, which works in the cold-chain and temperature-controlled logistics sector, subsequently became interested in the technology. The company is now working towards translating the laboratory material into a product for applications where maintaining temperature during storage and transport is critical.This could include packaging used to transport pharmaceuticals and other temperature-sensitive products. Such packaging needs to provide insulation while also being lightweight and strong enough to withstand handling and transportation. Its environmental impact after use is an increasing consideration as well.The move is the latest step in Bose’s broader work on more sustainable polymeric materials. His research has included efforts to find ways of reusing or upcycling plastics that are otherwise difficult to recycle, with the aim of keeping materials in use for longer rather than sending them to waste.For IISc, the foam's progress also shows the less visible part of academic innovation: getting a material developed in a laboratory into a form that industry can manufacture and customers can use. The licensing and scale-up process can require changes to the formulation, manufacturing process and product design even after the underlying research has been demonstrated.The next test, therefore, is whether the foam can be produced at commercial scale while retaining the insulation, strength and durability demonstrated during development. Its performance in actual cold-chain applications will ultimately determine whether the IISc innovation can become a practical alternative to conventional foams.For a material conceived around the problem of what happens to foam after its useful life, that commercial journey is as important as the laboratory breakthrough itself.Also read: IISc-Bengaluru creates eco-friendly packaging foamGet the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Google Maps renames Lake Ontario after Trump’s decree on ‘Lake America’
articles.summary: Tech giant says name to remain Lake Ontario for Canadian users, change reflects decision by US government agency.
articles.body:
Google has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America on its maps in the United States after an order by US President Donald Trump to rename the body of water as trade tensions escalate with Canada.

The tech giant said in a statement on Saturday that the name of the lake will be updated for US users but still appear as Lake Ontario in Canada. People outside the US and Canada will see both names.

Google said the decision reflects the change made by the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).

“These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now,” the company added.

Users in the US started reporting the update on Sunday.

Google followed a similar policy when Trump unilaterally renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America last year.

Apple Maps, which abided by Trump’s name change for the Gulf of Mexico, still shows the lake as Lake Ontario for users in the US as of Sunday.

The Trump administration on Thursday renamed the lake , which sits between the Canadian province of Ontario and the US state of New York, as a slight to Canada.

The US president had threatened to change the name of the lake as a retaliatory measure against Canada. Earlier this month, Trump imposed 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian products after the two countries failed to reach a trade agreement. Canada retaliated with similar levies.

On Wednesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney invoked the Indigenous roots of the name Ontario.

“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,'” he wrote in a social media post. “The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America.”

Carney added that while the US is changing its trade relationships, foreign policy and names of its bodies of water, “naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”

Over the past few days, Trump has shared several social media posts celebrating the name change.

He shared an AI-generated video on Saturday showing a flock of Canadian geese with his blond comb-over hairdo holding machineguns and patrolling “Lake America”. The post ends with the ducks firing their rifles in the air.

Trump’s critics have mocked the policy, arguing that the US is focused on trivial issues instead of tackling real problems that the country is facing, including the rising cost of living.

On Sunday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Trump’s order to rename the lake “was something out of Saturday Night Live”, a US comedy show created and produced by a Canadian.

“No one’s going to call it Lake America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue to be Lake Ontario,” Ford told the US network ABC News.

The controversy over the name of the lake came after the latest episode in the trade war between the US and Canada.

Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has been using tariffs to increase the price of imports from foreign countries as he seeks to remedy what he sees as an unfair imbalance with Washington’s trading partners.

Canada has historically been one of the closest allies of the US. But as the third largest exporter to the US, Canada has become one of the most persistent targets of Trump’s trade wars.

Beyond trade woes, Trump has repeatedly questioned Canada’s status as a sovereign country.

In the first months of his second term, Trump referred to then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau as governor, suggesting he was leading a US state, not an independent country.

Carney succeeded Trudeau in March 2025 with a platform focused on pushing back against Trump and helping Canada adjust to its changing relationship with the US.

articles.title: Israeli settlers storm Palestinian village, seizing home with owner inside
articles.summary: Israeli settlers stormed a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank on Saturday and seized a home while its owner was inside in the latest brazen settler attack in the area.
articles.body: Israeli settlers stormed a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank on Saturday and seized a home while its owner was inside in the latest brazen settler attack in the area. Despite the Israeli military saying there were “dozens of rioters” when they arrived at the scene, authorities have yet to announce any arrests as of Sunday evening. The settlers entered the village of Qusra early Saturday afternoon and began throwing stones at the home of Louay Adli, he told CNN. As he called Israeli police, the crowd swelled to what he estimated was 60 or 70 settlers. “They surrounded us from all sides and threw stones at all of us,” he said. “This went on for a whole hour until the army came from in front of the house, while the settlers were from behind.” Adli told CNN the Israeli army “watched and did nothing” before firing tear gas at the house. Video obtained by CNN appears to show a group of Israeli settlers hurling rocks at Adli’s house from one side of the building, while soldiers were operating on the other side. Adli says he and six others inside the home ran to the roof “because we could not breathe inside. We were suffocating and the army had us trapped with the settlers.” He said Israeli security forces later arrested and blindfolded him before warning him not to return to his own house. In response to CNN’s request for comment, the Israeli military said it used what it described as “proportionate force” against a Palestinian it accused of resisting and throwing stones. The official Israeli account acknowledged dozens of rioters were inside the Palestinian home, but did not say why they were able to leave without any arrests. “Security forces identified dozens of rioters who had barricaded themselves inside a Palestinian home while Palestinian residents were inside,” the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said in a joint statement with border police, before they “dispersed using various means.” Authorities seized three cars used as part of the raid, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a statement. But the IDF said the settlers “dispersed using various means” and that security forces are working “to locate those involved and hold them accountable in accordance with the law.” As of Sunday afternoon, authorities had not announced any arrests. A spokesman for Israel police said the investigation is ongoing as police work with authorities to gather additional evidence. Israeli President Isaac Herzog said the incident in Qusra was a “direct and flagrant defiance of the laws and values of the State of Israel. It is another incident in a disturbing sequence of events that casts a stain on Israel’s image and demands firm and decisive action.” In recent months, Israeli settlers have repeatedly besieged the village of Qusra, defying orders from the authorities to leave the area and trying to force Palestinian families, some of whom are also American citizens, out. US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called the settler violence a “horrific act of terror meant to intimidate and harass.” More than 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem. Most of the international community considers the settlements illegal under international law. Israel’s current right-wing government has made settlement expansion a central priority, advancing plans for thousands of new homes in the West Bank and approving scores of new settlements. NBC News crew attacked In a separate incident on Saturday in the West Bank town of Jalud, masked settlers attacked an NBC News crew as they were interviewing a Palestinian woman. The woman, Aida Ahmed Abdullah, told NBC News her family was forced out of their home by settlers. While the NBC crew was carrying out the interview, masked settlers drove up, attacking the team with sticks. “They jumped out, beat us, then jumped back in the car,” reported correspondent Matt Bradley, who was later treated at a nearby clinic. The Foreign Press Association condemned the attack and called for an investigation, saying in a statement, “This is not an isolated incident — it is part of a recurring pattern of violence against members of the press and Palestinian civilians.” Ayed Jafry, a Palestinian activist who works near Nablus, including the villages of Qusra and Jalud, told CNN the area was under threat of constant settler attacks. Often, he said, the military works with the settlers instead of stopping them. “The villages surrounding the city of Nablus are being targeted, specifically in these areas attacks happens on a daily basis,” he said. “The policy of displacement is clear, deliberate, and organized between the army and the settlers.” Israeli security forces said they were working to prevent further violence in the same area. “IDF soldiers and Israel Border Police forces continue to operate in the areas of Qusra and Jalud to prevent further disturbances and restore order in the area,” according to their joint statement. “The security forces strongly condemn all forms of violence.” Breaking his silence, Netanyahu condemned the incidents of settler violence while insisting it was only a “handful of rioters who are violating the law.” In a statement, he said authorities were “conducting a vigorous investigation on the ground, and I expect law enforcement authorities to arrest the rioters and bring them to justice as soon as possible.” But the settler violence has shown itself to be more widespread than a small band of extremists. On Thursday, IDF Chief of Staff. Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir said he had ordered the military to an elevated level of readiness In the West Bank because of escalating tensions. “Preparations must be made for the immediate deployment of units and battalions to reinforce the area,” Zamir ordered on Thursday. “The IDF, across all of its arrays, will maintain full, multi-front readiness throughout the holiday period - there will be no reduction in operational forces.”

articles.title: Google Maps will show ‘Lake America’ in U.S., not ‘Lake Ontario’
articles.summary: Google Maps has changed the name of “Lake Ontario” to “Lake America” for U.S. users to reflect President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming the lake, according to ​a Google statement.
articles.body: Google Maps has changed the name of “Lake Ontario” to “Lake America” for U.S. users to reflect President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming the lake, according to ​a Google statement. Trump announced on Thursday that he was changing the name ‌of the smallest of the five Great Lakes, part of an escalating trade feud with Canada that has prompted the two countries to impose reciprocal tariffs on billions of dollars ​in goods. The president’s order affects the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), which ​sets the standards for official U.S. maps. It does not have ⁠any impact on Canadian naming conventions or how the rest of the ​world refers to the lake. “Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in ​official government sources, which is GNIS for the U.S., people using Maps in the U.S. will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the ​U.S. and Canada will see both names,” Google said in a blog post ​issued on Saturday. The White House, Carney’s office and Ford’s office did not immediately comment on ‌Sunday ⁠on Google’s decision. Google Maps made a similar change to the Gulf of Mexico last year, labeling it the “Gulf of America” following Trump’s executive order on his first day in office renaming the body of water. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney immediately rejected ​the lake’s name ​change on Thursday. ⁠Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul of New York, which shares a long border with Canada, declared that “New York won’t be calling ​it that,” while Phil Scott, the Republican governor of neighboring ​Vermont, called ⁠Trump’s decision “petty and disappointing” on social media. The premier of Ontario, Doug Ford, on Saturday unveiled a large lakeside sign that reads, “Lake Ontario: Now and Always,” in both English ⁠and ​French. “President Trump can call it whatever he wants, ​but I can tell you, the rest of the world will always call it Lake Ontario,” Ford ​said.

articles.title: Death toll nears 800 after Himalayan glacier collapse
articles.summary: Specialised search-and-rescue teams join recovery operations in Nepal and China.
articles.body:
At least 797 people have been killed and 3,048 others remain missing after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayas, sending water and debris tearing through several villages.

Nepal announced an updated death toll of 781 on Sunday, with 2,502 people missing, including 592 foreign nationals. In China, state broadcaster CCTV reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing, including 261 foreigners.

The disaster occurred on Wednesday when part of a glacier at an altitude of roughly 5,200 metres (17,000 feet) collapsed, plunging around 1,200m (3,900ft) and gathering rock and debris before slamming into the Lende River.

Rescue operations have been suspended repeatedly since Friday due to poor weather and fears of fresh flooding. The disaster created a lake across the border between Nepal and China that has begun overflowing into Nepal’s Lhende and Trishuli Rivers.

More than 100 workers are also believed to be trapped inside several hydropower tunnels.

Authorities in Nepal began burying some of the victims on Sunday after taking DNA samples to allow for future identification. Many bodies were carried away by the floodwaters, leaving families unable to locate and identify their relatives. Mass burials for hundreds of unidentified victims are taking place in Nepal’s scenic Chitwan district, known for its forests and rivers.

According to the Red Cross, about 90,000 people in Nepal are likely affected by the disaster.

Specialised teams from India, China, and South Korea have joined the search-and-rescue efforts. Malaysia is also deploying its Special Malaysia Disaster Assistance Search and Rescue Team (SMART) and contributing $1m in recovery assistance.

International funding has begun to arrive, with the European Union promising $2.3m on Friday. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) has allocated more than $1m and launched an emergency appeal for $31m.

images.caption: Damaged buildings are seen partially buried under mud and debris near the swollen Trishuli River as rescue work is under way following landslides on August 30, 2026, in Trishuli Bazar, Nepal [Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images]

articles.title: School uniform swap shop 'helps save money and tackles second hand clothes stigma'
articles.summary: A free initiative which started with one school four years ago now has more than 200 involved.
articles.body:
A man who set up a uniform swap shop at his children's primary four years ago now has more than 200 schools involved.

Jon from Cardiff came up with the idea as a result of the cost-of-living crisis, to help parents with the financial burden of paying for a uniform which can run into hundreds of pounds.

From a plastic collection box outside Jon's house, the Free School clothes scheme has now launched a website and 8,000 items have been exchanged.

Jon says the website, which launched in March, has the potential to save Welsh families more than £50m a year in total.

Figures from the UK government put the average cost of a uniforms at about £343 annually for primary school children and £442 for a comprehensive pupil.

"If you've got more than one kid that's a significant additional cost to the family budget," said Jon.

"This free online swap shop built around the school community and families means they can list their good quality outgrown school clothes and offer them to other families within the school community for free and other families can then browse and request items and they can arrange a local collection of the items that they need.

"We always say second hand doesn't need to be mean second best."

Both Jon's children Tom, 10 and Sion, six, help their dad with sorting the clothes out.

Tom described the early days as "chaotic".

"The front room was just full of school clothes and there was a table with loads of clothes on and then more tables with more school clothes on them and I helped with sorting them by age and school," he said.

Almost half of parents said they're worried about the cost of school uniforms, according to research by the charity Save the Children and the Baby Bank Alliance network.

Elise, a mum of three, has just picked up a new uniform for her son Charlie.

"It's really expensive, I've got three kids you've got to get jumpers, T-shirts, trousers, shoes, double all of them because of the washing, so it's amazing for saving money but also I never buy anything new if I can help it because it seems such a waste when there's pre-loved which can be handed on."

Elise said she can always find what she needs through the scheme.

"You can say 'oh I'm really looking for some jumpers in age seven to eight or has anyone got the school uniform or the PE kit that we need' and nine times out of 10 somebody would be able to go 'oh yeah, I have actually I was going to pass that on or do something with it' and then we swap it over."

Jon started the scheme at his children's school, Ysgol Treganna in Cardiff in 2022, and still organises the swaps for the school, working with deputy head, Gareth Evans.

"At the end of each half term, myself and Tom will look at what's left in lost and found, basically what hasn't been reclaimed and then Tom and his group of friends will then bag everything up and take them home to Jon to add to the website," said Evans.

Jon's scheme isn't just about easing the financial strain on families, it's also about sustainability.

He said: "This is helping families to save both their pocket and the planet and I think that extra dimension around the environment has really captured people's interest in this initiative.

"There are 30,000 schools within the UK, all or most will be using school uniforms in one way shape or form, so the potential is definitely there to help many more schools.

"What matters most for me is the culture change and the change in sort of instinct around second-hand school clothes so that this becomes normal practice."

Kingsbury High School in London, which has 2,000 pupils, is involved in the scheme.

Tara Randall, the school's sustainability lead, says the initiative also takes away the stigma of asking for help with clothing your child and normalises swapping school clothes.

"There's a certain street cred that kids like to follow, especially at secondary school. But this is done in a discreet way, so there's no stigma.

"Parents can arrange their own drop-offs, pick-ups of uniforms, and, I guess the extra benefit on top of that is that you might find parents and carers from a community or connect in that kind of way, because it can feel very remote in secondary schools."

Some families qualify for a grant in Wales, offering up to £200 per child to cover the cost of school equipment, although it is only available to families on a low income or children in local authority care.

In England, from September uniforms will be limited to three items with a school logo, such as a blazer, jumper or sportswear plus a tie for secondary schools, to help parents save money.

articles.title: Four foods you should never store in the freezer and where to keep them instead
articles.summary: Chef Dennis Littley reveals why cheese, cooked pasta, cured meats and wine may lose texture and flavor when stored in the freezer after thawing.
articles.body: The freezer can help food last longer, but some kitchen staples may be better off stored elsewhere. Some foods can lose their texture, flavor or overall quality after being frozen and thawed, according to a recent list from food and cooking publication Food & Wine. New Jersey-based Chef Dennis Littley, a culinary educator and founder of Ask Chef Dennis, told Fox News Digital that freezing can change a food's texture because the water inside turns into ice crystals. SCIENTISTS SAY YOU'VE BEEN THROWING AWAY PERFECTLY GOOD MEAT BECAUSE OF ONE COMMON MISTAKE "The biggest thing I tell home cooks is that being able to freeze something doesn't necessarily mean you should," Littley said. Here are four foods that may be better stored somewhere other than the freezer. 1. Cheese While most cheeses can technically be frozen, Littley said doing so can leave them crumbly or grainy once thawed. The change can be particularly noticeable with softer and creamier cheeses. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Instead, Littley recommends keeping cheese well wrapped in the refrigerator and buying only as much as you expect to use while it is still fresh. 2. Cooked pasta Whether cooked pasta belongs in the freezer can depend on the dish. "Pasta can soften as it freezes and thaws, and creamy sauces can separate," Littley said. For pasta dishes with creamy sauces, he recommends refrigerating leftovers and eating them within a few days rather than freezing them. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Heartier baked pasta dishes, however, can hold up better in the freezer, according to Littley. 3. Cured meats Prosciutto, salami and other cured meats can generally be frozen, but Littley said the bigger concern is what happens to their texture and flavor afterward. That can be especially noticeable when the meat is served on a sandwich, charcuterie board or as an appetizer, where texture can be an important part of the experience. Littley recommends keeping cured meats wrapped in the refrigerator and using them within the recommended time after opening. 4. Wine Wine is one item Littley advises keeping out of the freezer. "No go," he said. "The liquid expands as it freezes, which can cause problems with the bottle or cork, and you're not doing the wine's flavor and aroma any favors." Instead, opened wine should be resealed and stored in the refrigerator, including red wine. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Red wine can then be brought back to the appropriate serving temperature before drinking, he said. While the freezer may seem like an easy way to extend the life of many foods and drinks, Littley said proper storage can help preserve their texture, flavor and overall quality. articles.title: Scottish Labour leadership contenders back North Sea drilling approval
articles.summary: Joe Fagan and Michael Marra were asked their views on the eve of voting on the contest to replace Anas Sarwar.
articles.body:
The two candidates in the Scottish Labour leadership race have called for new drilling licences in the North Sea to be approved "as soon as possible".

MSPs Joe Fagan and Michael Marra both said the Rosebank oil and Jackdaw gas fields offered cleaner methods of extraction than could be relied upon abroad, and that approval was vital to support jobs.

UK Labour ministers are set to make a decision on both projects after consultations closed in recent weeks.

The offshore industry has been lobbying hard, stressing the economic and energy security benefits, but environmentalist argue that more drilling is incompatible with efforts to tackle climate change.

Consultation ending on controversial Rosebank oil field

What is happening with the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields?

Marra and Fagan, the only two candidates to secure enough nominations to stand, are vying to replace Anas Sarwar after he announced he was joining Andy Burnham's UK government via the House of Lords.

Monica Lennon also wanted to stand, but failed to secure enough support from fellow Labour MSPs.

The candidates were asked for their views on the drilling licences by Press Association after a hustings in Stirling before voting in the contest begins on Monday.

Marra said the issue was "finely balanced" but he believed oil and gas could be produced in a cleaner way in the UK rather than by importing from abroad.

He said: "I want to see that decision as soon as possible, but I know that it's a challenging decision for the UK government."

Drilling would be "vital" for the north-east of Scotland as well as boosting public finances, he added.

"We need to move faster to make sure we can secure proper investment in the North Sea," he said.

Fagan also urged the UK government to approve the licences, saying there was a risk of offshore supply chains being "destroyed" if there was no movement.

"In fairness to the UK government, this isn't just a political decision, it's a legal decision as well," he said.

"They are bound by climate legislation. What's important for me is that they make that decision as soon as possible."

He said that if he won "I would put pressure on the UK government to make a decision quicker and to make the right decision for the Scottish and UK economy".

The winner of the leadership contest is due to be announced on Saturday 19 September.

The Rosebank oil field and the Jackdaw gas field, 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved under the previous Conservative government and construction is well under way.

But a legal challenge was brought at the Court of Session in Edinburgh in 2024 by campaign groups Uplift and Greenpeace UK which argued that consent was given without fully considering the impact of burning the fossil fuels which will be produced.

The previous decisions were ruled unlawful and sent back to the regulator Opred to be taken again.

Uplift has called on the UK government to reject the applications, insisting that more drilling will "wreck our planet" and result in more extreme weather.

Ultimately the decision is a quasi-legal one which will be taken by the regulator subject to final approval by the Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Although no timetable has been set for the final decision, the operator says a relatively quick decision could see the Jackdaw field producing gas by the winter.

articles.summary: DHS accused Brandon Johnson of punishing businesses that help ICE enforce federal immigration law after the Chicago mayor signed a new executive order.
articles.body: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson signed an executive order on Wednesday requiring city contractors to disclose information about leadership diversity demographics, as well as report whether they have any ties to certain law enforcement agencies such as ICE, as he moves to use the city's purchasing power to impose new contracting standards. Johnson said workplace data was necessary to identify discrimination and criticized the Trump administration's efforts to end federal reporting requirements. "If you want to do business with this city, we want to know whether the people leading your company reflect the diversity of the communities whose tax dollars are paying your contracts," Johnson said. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) accused Johnson of punishing American companies for assisting federal immigration enforcement. DEMOCRAT MAYOR BLASTED BY DHS FOR 'HUNTING DOWN' PROPERTY OWNERS LEASING TO ICE: 'UNHINGED' "If Mayor Johnson wants to lecture anyone about taxpayer dollars, remember what he is: a sanctuary politician who bullies American companies with money that isn’t his. Chicago takes the federal check, but it won’t enforce the federal law," a DHS spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital on Sunday. "In case Chicago’s mayor forgot, an oath of office is a commitment to upholding the law, not encouraging criminal illegal aliens to break it," they added. "Make no mistake, we will not be deterred. Under President Trump, ICE will keep enforcing the law in Chicago, whether City Hall likes it or not," the spokesperson said. The Chicago mayor unveiled the order during a press conference at Arise Chicago, a nonprofit that works to protect immigrants' rights. Johnson framed the order as a response to corporate influence in Washington and said Chicago would use city spending to put its values into practice. The order also directs Chicago's chief procurement officer to develop rules within 90 days barring vendors found to have committed public integrity, workplace discrimination or wage theft violations during the previous five years. Contractors must disclose whether they received more than $500,000 from government or law enforcement agencies or face proceedings alleging excessive force, unlawful detention, unconstitutional policing, discrimination or other civil rights violations. TRUMP ADMIN WANTS TO STOP ILLINOIS CITY'S REPARATIONS EFFORT FOR 'SIMPLY HANDING OUT MONEY BASED ON RACE' Large private companies with corporate families reporting at least $1 billion in net income must provide information about leadership diversity, board composition and diversity policies when not already covered by Illinois reporting law. Under the order, contractors must also report efforts to hire and promote formerly incarcerated people, and future awardees must update the disclosures at least annually. Doing business with ICE alone is not listed as a disqualifying offense. The order also disqualifies firms for specified integrity, discrimination or wage theft violations while making the disclosures public. Not With Our Money, the campaign that joined Johnson at the announcement, identified $3.19 billion in Chicago contractors held by 42 firms that also do business with ICE, according to the group's research. DHS ISSUES SCATHING REBUKE AFTER FORMER ATLANTA MAYOR KEISHA LANCE BOTTOMS TOUTS CUTTING TIES WITH ICE Johnson was referring to an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission proposal to rescind requirements for employers and other covered entities to file annual EEO reports containing aggregate employee race, sex and job-category data. EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas said the reports risked hindering enforcement of equal employment laws and raised constitutional concerns. The order marks Johnson’s latest clash with federal immigration authorities. In October, Johnson barred ICE from using city parking lots and garages for operations, a policy a federal agent said forced agents to stage in public and created operational risks. DHS said Operation Midway Blitz had resulted in more than 4,500 arrests by December. articles.title: Top officials from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan to meet in Istanbul
articles.summary: Foreign, defence ministers and military chiefs from three countries to meet for first time since signing Mecca pact.
articles.body:
Top officials from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan will gather in Istanbul on Monday for their first meeting since signing the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement earlier this month.

Turkish officials said on Sunday that the meeting will be attended by foreign ministers, defence ministers, and chiefs of staff from the three nations.

According to AFP, the Istanbul meeting will formally establish a “political and defence strategic committee” comprised of such national representatives.

Turkish Foreign Ministry sources, quoted by Reuters news agency, said the agenda will cover international security issues, as well as discussions on improving military cooperation and capabilities.

The Mecca agreement forms a collective security pact similar to NATO, under which an attack on one member could be considered an attack on all. The alliance was established following the United States-Israel war on Iran.

Turkiye possesses the second-largest military in NATO, Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim country, and Saudi Arabia is the world’s leading oil exporter.

In an August interview with Al Jazeera, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Egypt could potentially join the pact.

Bangladesh has also stated it is actively considering joining the agreement. The potential expansion is being closely monitored by India, whose Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Randhir Jaiswal, told reporters that New Delhi would take all necessary steps to safeguard its national security.

articles.title: A Phoenix concert promoter spent 50 years collecting music history; he is now selling more than 2,100 pieces to help feed cancer patients
articles.summary: US News: Veteran Phoenix concert promoter Danny Zelisko has put his personal music archive up for sale online, offering more than 2,100 pieces of memorabilia c.
articles.body: Veteran Phoenix concert promoter Danny Zelisko has put his personal music archive up for sale online, offering more than 2,100 pieces of memorabilia collected over five decades to help homebound cancer patients. The collection is being sold through an eBay storefront called Danny Zelisko’s Closet. It includes items gathered during more than 10,000 concerts he has produced throughout his career. Part of the money raised from the sales will go directly to The Joy Bus, a Phoenix-based non-profit that prepares and delivers fresh meals to people living with cancer. Reporting by radio station KTAR News 92.3 FM and local outlet Hoodline says the collection includes vintage tour T-shirts, signed photographs, original concert posters, backstage passes and ticket stubs dating back to the 1970s. "This isn't just memorabilia — it's a lifetime of memories," Zelisko said in an official statement about the sale. "Every poster, backstage pass, ticket and photograph has a story behind it."Rare items and prices across the archiveThe online store covers a wide range of prices, offering something for both casual fans and serious collectors. One of the lower-priced items is an R.E.M. backstage pass listed for $50. At the other end of the catalogue is a James Dean collection priced at $3,750. The package includes a signed photograph, commemorative stamps, an album and a guitar.Other notable items listed by KTAR News include:A 2008 Jonas Brothers package with an autographed guitar and tour poster priced at $2,275.A vintage 1993 Sade concert T-shirt listed for $2,000.A signed poster from rock band The Who priced at $700.Every item sold through the store comes with an official certificate of authenticity personally signed by Zelisko, confirming where the item came from.Five decades of Arizona concert historyZelisko began his career as a live music promoter after starting Evening Star Productions in Phoenix. In 1976, he began booking performers at Dooley’s Nightclub, a 750-capacity venue in Tempe. During the following two decades, the club hosted early Arizona shows by acts including The Police, KISS, Talking Heads and Nirvana. His work later expanded to major arenas and stadiums across Arizona, New Mexico and Las Vegas. During more than 50 years in the business, Zelisko produced concerts for major rock and pop stars including Pink Floyd, Paul McCartney, Billy Joel, Prince and Alice Cooper. His personal archive captures the growth of the Southwest concert scene, preserving physical reminders of everything from small club shows to large stadium tours.Funding meals for local cancer patientsMoney raised from the archive sale will help support The Joy Bus, which was founded in 2011 by Chopped champion chef Jennifer Caraway. She created the organisation in memory of her friend Joy Seitz-Butz, who died from ovarian cancer in 2012. The charity operates from a 6,700-square-foot facility in North Phoenix. The site includes a commercial kitchen, an organic food pantry and a public social-enterprise restaurant called The Joy Bus Diner. Profits from the diner and other fundraising efforts help pay for free, chef-prepared meals and home visits for people undergoing cancer treatment. According to health reporting by AZ Big Media, the non-profit received a $149,780 grant from Mercy C.A.R.E.S. earlier in the year. The funding will help expand its More Than a Meal Delivery Project, with a goal of reaching 2,500 home visits each week across the Valley. Zelisko, who is also a cancer survivor, has worked with the organisation before to support its nutrition programmes. As more items are added to the online store, collectors can buy pieces of Arizona’s music history while also helping provide food and support to vulnerable local residents.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Prisoners freed early are returning to jail at rapid rate, governors tell BBC
articles.summary: PM Andy Burnham on Sunday announced changes to the next early release scheme - scheduled to start in October - which mean PC Harper's killers will stay in jail.
articles.body:
Prisoners who were freed under the government's last early release scheme are returning to jail at a rapid rate, prison governors have told the BBC.

They say they are seeing the same inmates, who were let out as part of the 2024 early release scheme to ease overcrowding, coming back after reoffending - including for breaching their conditions.

"The churn is what stresses me out," said one governor in the Midlands, describing it as a "revolving door".

It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced changes to the next early release scheme, starting in October, following outrage that the killers of PC Andrew Harper were among those eligible to be released.

On Sunday, Burnham announced that they will not be, telling the BBC that anyone convicted of unlawful killing will be excluded from the scheme.

He conceded that it means "hundreds" more people will stay in prison - as prisons in England and Wales reach breaking point at more than 97% full.

The government says there are plans to create more prison space by deporting foreign inmates and releasing some who are serving indefinite sentences, but they are unlikely to create much more space by the time the first batch of inmates are released in October.

BBC News spoke to three serving prison governors in England to gauge the state of correctional facilities and how staff are dealing with overcrowding. Prison staff are not supposed to speak to the media so their names and the prisons they govern will not be mentioned to protect their identity.

One governor from a prison in the north of England said the PM's plans to ease overcrowding "is all short-term solutions and we need space now".

"Providing additional cells in existing prisons will mean more prison staff needed to monitor that - it's not easy," they said, adding that staff shortages mean "prisoners are not living in a safe and decent environment".

The governor also said they were frustrated by the rate of prisoner recalls, saying: "We see the same people coming back after being released early and reoffending again, or breaking their [release] rules."

Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost?

What's behind having to release some prisoners early?

There were 51,419 licence recalls in the year ending March 2026 - when a person is sent back to prison because they breached their release conditions or raised new risk concerns. The number went up from 40,259 in the previous year - a 28% increase.

Although recalls in January to March were slightly lower than the previous three-month period, they remain well above historical levels.

Another prison governor who also works in the north of England told the BBC that something needs to be done about overcrowding and prisoner recalls, or "the criminal justice system will grind to a halt".

"You release someone to serve the rest of their sentence in the community and you think 'now I have some extra room', but then they're back again and you just go round in circles.

"It's a big problem in the [men's prisons] and you worry that this is what will happen again when all these new people are let out."

As of March this year, more than 70,000 people had been released under the 2024 early release scheme.

But there are still almost 87,000 people in prisons across England and Wales - with just over 2,000 spaces remaining. With a backlog in the criminal courts of tens of thousands of cases, prison staff say that simply isn't enough space.

A rise in gang tensions within prisons is another impact of the overcrowding crisis, one of the governors from the north of England said.

They explained that due to the lack of space, more people from different parts of the country are being placed in the same facility, therefore increasing the chances of regional rivalries.

"When you've got inmates from Manchester and Liverpool for example, there is a worry there could be gang tension. Or having people from different parts of London could mean an escalation in threat levels because of rival gangs," they said.

"This has always happened, but it's happening more because so many prisons are full, and so people are sent to prisons far away," they added.

The lack of space has also led to cells, which are designed to hold one person, being used for two inmates, the other governor from northern England said, which raises "serious health and safety concerns".

"The single cells are small and they have a workspace for eating and an open toilet... so you're eating and going to the loo in a very small area and then you have to put another person in there and they're doing it all together," they said.

"Prisons are already dealing with an infestation issue and this could make it worse."

The BBC understands that work has begun to create more cells in prisons by re-purposing existing spaces, but that is expected to take months.

The prime minister had been under increasing pressure to block the early release of the killers of PC Harper, who died in 2019 when he was dragged by a car as three teenagers fled a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

There were concerns that two of them - Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole - may have been eligible for early release under the government's plan, and more than one million people signed a petition calling for them to remain behind bars.

As well as those convicted of manslaughter and murder, serious child sex offenders, rapists and groomers will not be eligible for early release under the new scheme as part of the Sentencing Act, as well as prisoners convicted of indecent assault offences and death by dangerous driving.

On Tuesday, the justice secretary is expected to give further details, including how many people will be affected, during a statement to Parliament.

For one of the prison governors in the north of England, the situation is at breaking point. They said some inmates must be set free for capacity reasons, but ministers need to look at wider maintenance issues, too.

"We've got to alleviate the pressure somehow or we will break... But prison spaces could be made available if we maintained buildings properly," they explained. "We have too many cells we can't use because there's something wrong with them which seems ridiculous when you have an overcrowding crisis."

The governor said England's prisons have not been properly maintained for decades, and the problems have snowballed, creating "fragile infrastructure regularly breaking and preventing proper regimes from operating".

"If prisons are full, you can't carry out big maintenance projects and you lose those spaces. It's unsustainable. It's like having a car that you have to drive 24/7. If you don't service it and run it constantly you shouldn't be surprised if it fails and can't be fixed."

Tom Wheatley, president of the Prison Governors Association (PGA) told the BBC that no governors had been briefed on the government's plans to ease overcrowding.

"How are we supposed to deal with angry and confused prisoners when we find out about the plans last minute?" he asked.

A 2024 National Audit Office report concluded that "over the next few years there will be continued risk to the capacity in prisons, because of the poor condition of parts of the estate".

It said that "a quarter (23,000) of prison places do not meet fire safety standards".

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "Less than one in seven prisoners in custody are on recall, and it is a vital tool to keep the public safe.

"This government inherited prisons in crisis but we are fixing this, reforming the length of time people spend on recall to reduce the prison population, building 14,000 new places, launching the biggest ever expansion of tagging, and giving victims a say in the strict licence conditions of offenders."

articles.title: Photos: Devastation from the Nepal-China floods
articles.summary: More than 3,000 people missing after glacier collapse unleashes destruction in Himalayas.
articles.body:
At least 797 people have been killed, and more than 3,000 remain missing after a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas triggered catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border.

The torrent tore through the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi river systems on Wednesday, sweeping away villages, roads and hydropower projects and carrying bodies as far as India.

In Nepal alone, hundreds of hydropower workers remain unaccounted for and roughly 93,000 people have been affected as rescue teams contend with collapsed bridges, blocked tunnels and new landslides.

articles.title: Workers restoring a medieval English house found 800 years of hidden history, including rare wall paintings, sealed doorways and mysterious protective marks
articles.summary: UK News: A conservation project at Dunstable’s Grade II listed Priory House has uncovered 800 years of hidden history, including nationally important wall pain.
articles.body: A conservation project at Dunstable’s Grade II listed Priory House has uncovered 800 years of hidden history, including nationally important wall paintings, sealed medieval doorways and protective marks once used to keep evil spirits away. Specialist teams led by HB Archaeology & Conservation Limited, together with structural engineers and building contractors, have been working since 2022 to repair and strengthen the ageing building. The major restoration project is supported by £1,142,730 from The National Lottery Heritage Fund and £684,312 from Historic England. The discoveries have also changed what historians know about the building’s past.Scientific tests confirm 13th-century originsScientific tests on organic material found inside the building’s vaulted stone undercroft confirmed that the structure dates from the early-to-mid 13th century. Radiocarbon testing of twigs found above the vaulting cones dated them to between cal AD 1217 and 1269. The undercroft was originally part of Dunstable Priory and was used as a guest house for travellers and pilgrims travelling along the ancient Watling Street. Archaeologists also found evidence of the building’s earliest layout. Among the discoveries was a forgotten doorway that once connected the main High Street directly to the inner priory grounds. They also found the original central hearth, which provided heat to the room above the stone vault. After King Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries in 1540, the building was separated from the church estate and turned into a private high-status home.Five layers of historic wall paintings foundThe removal of later plasterboard and panelling from the first floor revealed several layers of wall decoration from different periods. Dr Andrea Kirkham, a specialist in wall paintings and historic stone conservation, found up to five separate decorative schemes on the same wall. The surviving paintings range from 16th-century Tudor designs to 17th-century Jacobean patterns, showing how later owners repeatedly changed and updated the rooms. Conservator Claudia Fiocchetti carried out urgent work to protect the fragile paint and prevent further damage while repairs continued on the timber structure behind the walls. Conservators also found remains of late 18th-century hand-printed wallpaper and fabric wall coverings. In the attic, workers discovered pieces of woven straw plaiting that had been thrown away. The material confirms the building’s 19th-century link to the commercial straw-hat industry, when the site was used as a workshop by the firm Munt & Brown.Protective symbols carved into old timberThe restoration team also recorded apotropaic marks, commonly called "witch marks", carved into wooden beams and stonework around the building. The symbols include interlocking circles and marks made by burning candles into the surfaces. People who lived in the building believed these signs could protect their homes from witchcraft, fire and harmful spirits. These protective marks were often placed near entrances, including chimney flues, windows and doorways. People believed such points could allow evil forces to enter the home. In a statement published by Dunstable Town Council, the building’s current custodians described their surprise at the discoveries: "When Dunstable Town Council embarked on the repairs to Priory House back in 2022 as current custodians we thought we knew all that we could know about this remarkable building, but it turns out that it was hiding much more than we could ever have imagined," the council stated. The local authority said the restoration has taken longer than first expected because the building requires complex conservation work. However, the discoveries have provided important information about how the structure changed over eight centuries.Future opening and community heritageHistoric England and The National Lottery Heritage Fund said the historic objects and architectural features found during the project will be kept in place wherever possible. The new discoveries are also being included in updated heritage information and educational displays. These will help shape what visitors see and learn when the Grade II* listed building reopens. According to updated plans from Dunstable Town Council, Priory House is expected to complete its structural conservation work and fully reopen as a community heritage hub and tourist information centre in early 2027.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump vows to report NBC anchor Kristen Welker to FCC over 'purposeful inaccuracy' on endorsements
articles.summary: Trump announced on Truth Social that Kristen Welker will be reported to the FCC after she described his primary endorsement record as mixed results.
articles.body: President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that NBC's "Meet the Press" host Kristen Welker would be reported to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for potential punishment after she characterized his primary endorsement record as producing mixed results. "Kristen Welker, the Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press, now considered Meet the Fake Press, just stated that Donald Trump has ‘mixed results’ on his Endorsements of Candidates, when the recent WINS of Darline Graham and Mike Mazzei, stand at 100% for the U.S. Senate, and 98% for the U.S. House, recently and over the longterm," Trump said in a post on Truth Social. "How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves? Results are attached," Trump continued. "Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment. Unfortunately, she is not the only one." NBC News defended Welker in a statement to Fox News Digital on Sunday, backing its "Meet the Press" moderator following Trump’s threat. TRUMP STORMS OFF 'MEET THE PRESS' INTERVIEW, RIPS WELKER, ABC, CBS, CNN AS 'CROOKED' "Kristen is one of the best in the business and we stand by her," an NBC News spokesperson said. Welker did not make the remark during Sunday’s "Meet the Press" broadcast. She made it earlier on Sunday during a live preview appearance on NBC4 Washington, saying Trump had endorsed "a slate of candidates in the primaries" and "had some mixed results." Welker, citing NBC reporting, predicted Trump would "loom large" over the midterms and immediately cited Darline Graham's primary victory as his most recent endorsement success. "He’s going to loom large over these midterms. There's no doubt about that. He, of course, has endorsed a slate of candidates in the primaries. He's had some mixed results, but most recently, his pick of Senator Darline Graham, of course, the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, was successful in her primary battle, so now she takes on Dr. Annie Andrews in South Carolina," Welker said. FROM ABC LICENSE REVIEWS TO COMEY INDICTMENTS, TRUMP'S REGULATORY WAR ON CRITICS ENTERS NEW PHASE CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter criticized Trump’s demand Sunday, characterizing it as an effort to use the FCC against a journalist over unfavorable coverage. "Trump is getting more explicit about weaponizing the FCC. This morning he said @kwelkernbc will be ‘reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment’ for saying something he didn’t like about his endorsement record. (By law, the FCC can’t punish Welker.) And that’s not all..." Stelter posted to X. A Fox News Trump Primary Endorsement Tracker published Thursday found Trump-backed candidates had won all 24 Republican Senate primaries in which he endorsed and 214 of 218 House primaries, producing a 100% Senate success rate and a roughly 98% House rate. The two victories Trump identified came Tuesday. Graham defeated Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina’s Senate runoff, while former state Sen. Mike Mazzei defeated Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond by approximately 2,000 votes for the Republican gubernatorial nomination. The Fox News tracker recorded victories for 16 of Trump's 21 gubernatorial picks. His five defeated candidates included Pamela Evette in South Carolina, Mike Lindell in Minnesota and Megan Degenfelder in Wyoming. TRUMP ENDORSEMENT FAILS TO CLEAR GOP FIELD AS FORMER GOVERNOR JOINS SOUTH CAROLINA SENATE RACE Trump accused news organizations of using his losses to discount a broader record he described as historically strong. "Their new weapon is to say that my 99% SUCCESS Rate on Endorsements, 100% on Senatorial Endorsements (Many of whom were not even given a shot of winning until I Endorsed!), is either a mixed result, or not very good. In actuality, it is, without question, the strongest Endorsement in the History of Politics," Trump said. He ended his post by appealing directly to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. FCC CHAIR SUGGESTS ABC SKIPPING TRUMP'S SPEECH WILL FACTOR IN LICENSE RENEWAL DECISION "The Press is a Disgrace to our Nation, and I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously," Trump said. Carr has previously warned broadcasters that news distortion could affect license renewals. The FCC, however, licenses individual stations rather than networks such as NBC, and its published policy requires evidence that a report was deliberately intended to mislead viewers, distinguishing deliberate distortion from an inaccuracy or difference of opinion.
